notes: Prison disciplinary JR on racist language charge; Governor's post-hoc witness statement and new grounds refused.

enrichment.short_title: Gleaves: judicial review of prison racist language adjudication
key_facts: Roger Gleaves, a category B prisoner at HMP Whitemoor, was found guilty of using racist words contrary to Prison Rule 51(20A) after calling or mimicking in a German accent near education staff member Ms MacGuinness.
The Governor admitted expert evidence from a Race Relations Liaison Officer and found the charge proved regardless of the prisoner's intentions.
The Secretary of State upheld the adjudication; permission for judicial review was granted only on whether the Governor found Gleaves had called Ms MacGuinness a 'Kraut'.
Form F256 did not record why the Governor rejected the defence or required questions to be put through her.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Secretary of State's decision upholding a prison disciplinary finding, with a renewed application to raise further grounds refused.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the Governor's later witness statement was accepted as credible and the challenge to the finding of guilt failed; permission to raise two new grounds was refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where no statutory duty to give reasons applies, a Governor's post-proceedings witness statement may be relied on if consistent with the record and not a retrospective justification; inappropriate expert evidence on racist offensiveness does not vitiate a finding if guilt would otherwise be established beyond reasonable doubt.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator made a finding that the prisoner called the victim a Kraut
Whether the Governor adequately considered mens rea and the prisoner's defence
Whether reliance on expert evidence on racial offensiveness was lawful
Whether late grounds relating to questioning procedure should be permitted
linked_authorities: R (Nash) v Chelsea College of Art and Design (2001) The Times 25 July
R v Board of Visitors ex parte McConkey (1982) The Times 23 September

confidence.notes: Procedural history, legal framework and final dismissal are clearly recorded.

notes: Attorney General reference on lenient community orders for domestic assaults; leave refused.

enrichment.short_title: AG Ref 95/2004: unduly lenient domestic violence community orders
key_facts: A 51-year-old former police officer was convicted after trial of two assaults occasioning ABH and one indecent assault against his former partner over several years.
He received community punishment orders totalling 80 hours rather than immediate custody.
The trial judge found the relationship volatile with aggression on both sides and that the offences were not part of a campaign of violence.
The Solicitor General sought leave to refer the sentence as unduly lenient.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 alleging unduly lenient sentences following a seven-day Crown Court trial.
enrichment.outcome: Leave to refer refused; the sentence was lenient but within the judge's discretion given mitigation, findings of fact and the seriousness of the offences.
enrichment.ratio: Good character and public service may mitigate sentences for domestic violence; relationship context and property damage by the victim are relevant factual matters; a lenient sentence is not unduly lenient merely because custody might otherwise have been imposed.
legal_issues: Whether community orders were unduly lenient for domestic assaults
Whether public service and good character are mitigating in domestic violence cases
Whether bilateral aggression negates aggravating features
Relevance of pending Sentencing Advisory Panel consultation on domestic violence
linked_authorities: Attorney-General's Reference No 98 of 2002 [2003] EWCA Crim 1018
Attorney-General's Reference No 22 of 2002 [2002] EWCA Crim 1500
R v Millberry [2003] 2 Cr App R(S) 142

confidence.notes: Facts, mitigation analysis and refusal of leave are explicit.

notes: Negligence appeal dismissed; Down's Syndrome claimant found competent to cross busy road to minibus.

enrichment.short_title: Slater v Buckinghamshire: minibus collection negligence appeal
key_facts: Paul Slater, a 25-year-old with Down's Syndrome, was knocked down crossing Boundary Road to reach a council-contracted minibus and suffered tetraplegic injuries.
For about five years the established practice was for Paul to cross the busy road himself to the pick-up point on the far side, sometimes collected by escort Mrs Brooks if late.
On the accident day a Royal Mail van obscured visibility; Mrs Brooks told Paul to wait but he ran into traffic.
Morland J found Paul had road safety competence and neither the council nor the contractor was negligent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from trial judgment dismissing negligence claims against Buckinghamshire County Council and minibus contractor Stigwood.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge's finding that Paul could safely cross the road at rush hour and that the collection system was reasonably safe was upheld.
enrichment.ratio: A local authority and contractor owe a duty to take reasonable care in transporting disabled clients, but where a claimant has demonstrated competence to cross a road safely over hundreds of prior occasions, a flexible pick-up system allowing independent crossing is not necessarily negligent.
legal_issues: Whether the collection system exposed Paul to foreseeable risk
Whether contractual specifications required door-to-door collection
Whether pleadings precluded findings on road safety competence
Whether the judge's fact-finding on competence was open on the evidence
linked_authorities: Re-Source American International Ltd v Platt Site Services [2004] EWCA Civ 665

confidence.notes: Detailed fact findings and appellate deference to the trial judge are clearly reasoned.

notes: Child support housing costs appeal; short remortgage term held necessarily incurred after divorce.

enrichment.short_title: Pabari: child support exempt income and mortgage housing costs
key_facts: Mr Pabari remortgaged the matrimonial home after divorce to pay a £56,000 lump sum and transfer endowment policies to his former wife.
He chose a 12-year repayment mortgage keeping the prior redemption date rather than a longer 25-year term, reducing child maintenance assessments.
Mrs Pabari appealed contending only repayments on a normal 25-year mortgage were 'necessarily incurred' housing costs under Schedule 3 paragraph 4(1)(a).
The child support commissioner upheld the shorter term as necessarily incurred in context of continuity of occupation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a child support commissioner on the meaning of 'necessarily incurred' housing costs in maintenance assessment regulations.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the commissioner's judgment that the 12-year mortgage costs were necessarily incurred was within reasonable bounds.
enrichment.ratio: 'Necessarily incurred' in Schedule 3 paragraph 4(1)(a) of the MASC Regulations sets a high but not absolute threshold; remortgaging after divorce to retain the same home and redemption date may qualify even without extending the mortgage term.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'necessarily incurred' for eligible housing costs
Whether mortgage term and amount are relevant to housing cost eligibility
Application of Moyna v Secretary of State for Work and Pensions to imprecise statutory tests
Conflict between commissioner decisions on remortgage term reductions
linked_authorities: Moyna v Secretary of State for Work and Pensions [2003] UKHL 44
R v Monopolies and Mergers Commission, ex parte South Yorkshire Transport [1993] 1 WLR 23

confidence.notes: Statutory framework and appellate deference on 'necessarily' are thoroughly analysed though outcome is fact-sensitive.

notes: Children relocation appeal allowed; recorder misapplied Payne v Payne and preferred contact over mother's Spain move.

enrichment.short_title: Re S (Children): relocation to Spain appeal allowed
key_facts: Following divorce, the mother sought permission to relocate with two young daughters from Halifax to Alicante where her extended family lived.
The father commuted weekly to Hamburg for work and opposed the move, arguing contact would be unaffordable and the plan unrealistic.
The recorder found the mother's plan genuine and practical but refused permission primarily because contact would be expensive.
The Court of Appeal found internal inconsistencies and a misdirection treating the case as a mere lifestyle choice.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a county court recorder's refusal of permission to remove children permanently from the jurisdiction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; relocation permission granted subject to contact arrangements being settled first; no full retrial ordered.
enrichment.ratio: Payne v Payne principles apply where a primary carer seeks to return to family support after a short marriage in an area with no ties; refusal based on contact costs is inconsistent with favourable findings on the mother's credibility and the father's negative case.
legal_issues: Application of Payne v Payne to relocation after short marriage
Whether the move was a lifestyle choice or isolation-driven return to family
Whether the recorder's contact-cost reasoning was inconsistent with his findings
Whether to remit for retrial or decide the relocation issue on appeal
linked_authorities: Payne v Payne [2001] EWCA Civ 166

confidence.notes: Detailed analysis of the recorder's findings and clear allowance of appeal.

notes: Green belt planning appeal quashed for inadequate reasons on very special circumstances and contamination.

enrichment.short_title: Dowmunt-Iwaszkiewicz: green belt contamination planning challenge
key_facts: The claimant owned a 6.17-acre former mushroom farm in Nottingham green belt contaminated with asbestos in derelict buildings.
Outline planning permission for up to five residential dwellings was refused and an appeal dismissed on green belt and openness grounds.
The claimant argued asbestos removal required development proceeds and constituted very special circumstances.
The inspector acknowledged public interest in remediation but gave inadequate reasons for rejecting very special circumstances.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 challenge to an inspector's decision dismissing a planning appeal determined on written representations.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded on the very special circumstances ground; the inspector's decision was quashed for failure to give adequate reasons and carry out a visible balancing exercise.
enrichment.ratio: Where contamination remediation is argued as very special circumstances for inappropriate green belt development, the inspector must explain why those circumstances are insufficient and show how harm to the green belt was weighed against remediation benefits per South Bucks v Porter.
legal_issues: Whether contamination alone can amount to very special circumstances
Correct interpretation of Circular 02/2000 paragraph 20
Adequacy of reasons for rejecting very special circumstances
Impact of proposed development on green belt openness
linked_authorities: South Bucks District Council v Porter (No 2) [2004] UKHL 33

confidence.notes: Quashing on reasons ground is clear; openness challenge was not upheld.

notes: SEN statement appeal partly allowed; Part 3 failed to specify occupational therapy provision.

enrichment.short_title: C v East Sussex: special educational needs statement challenge
key_facts: An 11-year-old boy with profound language disorder and significant motor skills difficulties had a Statement of Special Educational Needs naming Peacehaven School.
Parents wanted placement at Moor House School; SENDIST upheld Peacehaven and specified one hour weekly speech therapy.
Part 2 identified dyspraxia and sensory integration difficulties but Part 3 did not specify how occupational therapy needs would be met.
At the time of hearing no individual occupational therapy had been provided beyond general school support.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 11 of the Tribunals and Inquiries Act 1992 against a SENDIST decision amending a statement of special educational needs.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; Part 3 was defective for failing to specify occupational therapy provision; speech and language therapy specification was upheld.
enrichment.ratio: A statement of special educational needs must in Part 3 identify not only objectives but the means by which significant motor skills deficits will be addressed; failure to do so prevents enforcement and assessment of provision.
legal_issues: Whether Part 3 adequately specified occupational therapy provision
Whether one hour weekly direct speech therapy was adequate for profound language disorder
Adequacy of SENDIST reasons on therapy quantum
Form of relief without quashing the whole statement
linked_authorities: R (L) v London Borough of Waltham Forest [2003] EWHC 2907 (Admin)
Staffordshire County Council v J [1996] ELR 418

confidence.notes: Split outcome on OT versus speech therapy grounds is clearly explained.

notes: Section 151 RTA appeal allowed; homeward journey after fare ended remained social domestic pleasure use.

enrichment.short_title: Keeley v Pashen: motor insurance limitation of use and section 151
key_facts: Mini-cab driver Edward Pashen, insured for social domestic and pleasure use only, drove at passengers after an altercation following his last fare, killing Terence Keeley.
He pleaded guilty to manslaughter; the policy excluded use for hire or reward.
The judge held Pashen was not on a hire-or-reward journey but also not on a social domestic pleasure journey when he reversed and drove at the men.
The widow claimed psychiatric injury and sought enforcement against insurers under section 151.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a county court preliminary issue determining insurers' liability under section 151 of the Road Traffic Act 1988.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and cross-appeal dismissed; insurers were liable because after the last fare the essential character of the journey was driving home, a covered use, despite an incidental attempt to frighten the passengers.
enrichment.ratio: Under Seddon v Binions the essential character of the journey governs limitation-of-use clauses; driving home after the final fare remains social domestic and pleasure use even if the driver briefly deviates to frighten former passengers.
legal_issues: Whether Pashen was using the car for hire or reward at the time of the accident
Whether reversing to frighten passengers was a separate uncovered journey
Application of the essential character test from Seddon v Binions
Enforceability of section 151 rights by an innocent third party
linked_authorities: Seddon v Binions [1978] 1 Lloyd's Rep 381
Gardner v Moore [1984] AC 548
Caple v Sewell [2001] EWCA Civ 1848

confidence.notes: Agreed facts and application of established insurance law principles are straightforward.

notes: Loosely entrapment appeal allowed; addict-only supplier prosecution stayed as state-created crime.

enrichment.short_title: R v Moon: entrapment and abuse of process for heroin supply
key_facts: Diana Moon, a heroin addict with no dealing history, supplied £10 of heroin to undercover officer Jackie at Cambridge bus station after repeated approaches.
The Crown accepted she was an addict only, not a dealer or runner; she bought the drugs from another supplier without profit.
No authorisation was given under the undercover operations Code of Practice; Jackie admitted she caused an offence that would not otherwise have occurred.
The recorder rejected the abuse of process application but treated Moon as willing to supply regular customers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction for possession with intent to supply following a voir dire rejecting a stay for entrapment and abuse of process.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction on count 1 quashed; prosecution should have been stayed as unfair state-created crime.
enrichment.ratio: Under R v Loosely, prosecuting an addict-only supplier whom undercover officers persistently induced to commit a one-off supply, without predisposition, proper authorisation or evidence she would otherwise have supplied, is an abuse of process.
legal_issues: Whether the undercover operation caused rather than merely afforded opportunity for the offence
Relevance of absent predisposition and lack of dealing history
Effect of missing Code of Practice authorisation
Whether the recorder erred in preferring the officer's evidence over the appellant's
linked_authorities: R v Loosely [2001] UKHL 53
Nottingham City Council v Amin [2000] 1 Cr App R 426

confidence.notes: Crown concession on addict status and detailed Loosely analysis support a clear outcome.

notes: VAT repayment trader JR; proportionality guidance given but no pre-determination interest entitlement.

enrichment.short_title: UK Tradecorp: VAT input tax repayment investigation and proportionality
key_facts: UK Tradecorp, a repayment trader dealing in high-value zero-rated goods linked to missing trader intra-Community fraud, claimed £2.57m input tax repayments in 2003.
Customs thoroughly investigated suspicious transactions; most claims were paid after delay, with one month still disputed at tribunal.
The claimant sought declarations on proportionality and entitlement to LIBOR interest from the date claims were submitted.
Lightman J held repayment entitlement arises only once claims are accepted or established, not on submission.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review with permission granted seeking declarations on Customs' duties when verifying VAT repayment claims.
enrichment.outcome: No relief granted; proportionality duty acknowledged; no entitlement to interest before acceptance or establishment of claims; guidance given on balancing factors.
enrichment.ratio: Customs must investigate repayment claims proportionately and maintain judicial control, but Molenheide does not require interest from claim submission; prima facie repayment rights arise only when input tax claims are admitted or upheld.
legal_issues: Whether the Commissioners must act proportionately in VAT repayment investigations
When the right to deduct and receive repayment arises under the Sixth VAT Directive
Whether interest is payable from claim submission or only after acceptance
Division of jurisdiction between the High Court and VAT tribunal
linked_authorities: Garage Molenheide BVBA [1998] STC 126
Capital One Developments Ltd v CCE [2002] STC 479
R (Deluni Mobile Ltd) v CCE [2004] EWHC 1030

confidence.notes: Extensive legal analysis though fact-intensive proportionality disputes were not adjudicated.
